PART 7 — The Critics: "Don't Forgive Without Repentance"

7.1 The Conditional-Forgiveness Position, Stated Fully

A real and sincerely-held position among biblical counselors and theologians holds that biblical forgiveness is conditional on the offender's repentance, modeled directly on how God forgives. Their case, stated as strongly and fairly as possible:

  • Luke 17:3-4 explicitly conditions the command: "If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him." The grammar itself makes repentance the hinge.
  • Matthew 18:15-17 lays out a process of confrontation that assumes forgiveness and restored relationship follow repentance, not blanket unconditional acceptance regardless of response — otherwise the entire confrontation process (go to him privately, then with witnesses, then to the church) would be pointless.
  • God's own pattern: throughout Scripture, divine forgiveness is repeatedly tied to confession and repentance (1 John 1:9; 2 Chron 7:14; Luke 15's prodigal does turn and come home before the embrace is described in full, even if the father runs first). "Forgive as God forgave you" (Eph 4:32) might then mean forgive the way God forgives — in response to turning — not regardless of it.
  • Pastoral and justice concerns: teaching unconditional forgiveness, critics argue, can be used to pressure abuse victims back into danger, can let unrepentant offenders off the hook relationally and spiritually, and can function as a kind of cheap grace that treats sin too lightly.

This is not a fringe or careless position — it reflects a real exegetical argument and a real pastoral concern that deserves to be taken seriously, not dismissed.

7.2 The Relational / Unconditional-Release Position, Stated Fully

The relational gospel framework this series has used, and most trauma-informed Christian counseling, distinguishes inner release (what Part 4.5 called forgiveness) from relational restoration (reconciliation) — and argues Scripture itself supports unconditional release as a distinct act from conditional reconciliation:

  • Luke 23:34 — Jesus, from the cross, prays "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" while being crucified by soldiers who had shown no repentance whatsoever, mid-offense. This is the clearest biblical model of forgiveness preceding, not following, repentance.
  • Acts 7:60 — Stephen, being stoned, prays "Lord, do not hold this sin against them" — again, no repentance has occurred; the offense is actively ongoing.
  • Romans 5:8, 10 — "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us... while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God" — the foundational act is explicitly prior to, not contingent on, repentance; God's love and the provision of forgiveness precede the human turning that receives it.
  • Colossians 3:13 / Ephesians 4:32 — "forgiving each other... as the Lord forgave you" can equally be read as forgive in the same generous, initiating spirit God showed, which Rom 5:8 has already defined as prior to repentance, not strictly "only once they've repented."
  • Hebrews 12:15 warns that a root of bitterness, left untended, "springs up and defiles many" — a warning addressed to the hurt person's own soul, independent of whether the offender ever repents, implying some kind of release is needed regardless.

7.3 Reconciling the Two: Two Different Referents for One English Word

The apparent contradiction dissolves once Part 4's lexical distinctions are applied carefully. Both camps are often correct about what they are each actually describing — they are using the single English word "forgiveness" for two different biblical realities:

Attitudinal / inner release (aphiemi as internal act)Transactional / relational forgiveness (aphiemi as restored standing)
What it isReleasing your own claim and bitterness before God — Part 4.5's "forgiveness"A declared, relational release of the matter between two parties — closer to what Part 4.5 called reconciliation
Luke 17:3-4 fits here?Not primarily — this text is about restored fellowship/standing after confrontation, i.e., closer to reconciliation languageYes — this is exactly a two-party, repentance-conditioned process
Luke 23:34 fits here?Yes — Jesus releases his own claim against people still mid-offenseNo — nothing is being claimed about restored relationship with the soldiers
Required of the hurt person always?YesNo — depends on the offender's genuine metanoia (Part 4.2)

The relational gospel's resolution: you are always called to the inner release (Luke 23:34's pattern) — this is not optional, and Hebrews 12:15 treats failing to do it as spiritually dangerous to you. You are never required to extend the second, relational sense — restored trust and standing — to someone who has not turned (metanoia, not metamelomai). Luke 17:3-4 and Matthew 18 are genuinely, rightly describing that second, conditional process; they are simply not describing the same thing Jesus does on the cross. Both camps' key texts remain fully true; they were never actually in conflict once "forgiveness" is allowed to mean two related but distinct things, exactly as Part 4's word study demonstrated.

7.4 Answering the Specific Objections

ObjectionResponse
"Unconditional forgiveness enables abusers and lets them avoid consequences."Part 4.5 and 6.1 directly separate forgiveness from consequences and from reconciliation. Releasing your internal claim against someone (Rom 12:19 hands justice to God, it does not cancel it) is fully compatible with pursuing legal consequences, church discipline, or permanent no-contact. Forgiveness never requires silence about ongoing danger (Part 6.3's abuse cases).
"This cheapens sin and grace — 'cheap grace.'" (echoing Dietrich Bonhoeffer's famous warning)Bonhoeffer's target was grace detached from any call to discipleship or cost. Inner release is not costless — Part 2 and Part 5.3 show it is often a long, costly, re-chosen process, and it still fully expects repentance and consequence on the offender's side for reconciliation (the second sense) to follow. Nothing about Part 7.3's resolution tells the offender their sin doesn't matter.
"Jesus's prayer on the cross and Stephen's prayer were unique, exceptional acts, not a model for ordinary people."Possible, but the text gives no explicit signal marking them as non-repeatable; Stephen was a deacon, not an apostle, which weakens the case that this was an apostolic-office-only act. At minimum, they stand as the clearest positive biblical examples of forgiveness preceding repentance, which the conditional-only reading has to explain away rather than simply set aside.
"The Bible only commands forgiveness in response to repentance (Luke 17:3-4), so unconditional forgiveness is not actually commanded."True of that specific passage's content (Part 7.3's table) — but Hebrews 12:15, Mark 11:25 ("whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone" — no repentance clause present at all), and the cross/Stephen examples show the New Testament's forgiveness vocabulary is not used in only one conditional sense throughout.
"This is therapeutic self-help dressed up as theology, prioritizing the victim's feelings over biblical justice."A fair challenge to weigh honestly. The reply: releasing bitterness for your own sake (Heb 12:15) is explicitly in Scripture's own interest, not imported from psychology — psychology has simply independently confirmed (Part 2.3) what Hebrews already warned about. And this framework does not set feelings above justice; Part 6's whole structure keeps consequences, safety, and reconciliation strictly tied to the offender's actual repentance, which is the opposite of therapeutic relativism.

7.5 What To Do With Someone Who Never Repents

  1. Do the inner release anyway (Part 5.3's steps; Luke 23:34's pattern) — this is for your own freedom and spiritual health (Heb 12:15), not a verdict on them.
  2. Hand the justice question to God explicitly (Rom 12:19) — this is not passive resignation; it is a deliberate transfer of a burden you were never equipped to carry.
  3. Maintain appropriate boundaries and consequences — forgiveness does not require continued exposure, silence, or pretending nothing happened (Part 6.4).
  4. Grieve what will not be restored — some relationships do not reconcile in this life; Scripture allows real lament over this (Part 1.3), not forced positivity.
  5. Keep the door — not necessarily the relationship — open: continuing to pray for the person's genuine metanoia (not their punishment) keeps you from hardening (Part 2.3's "hardened heart" pattern) while still requiring nothing premature of you.
  6. Find community that understands the distinction — a church or counselor who conflates forgiveness with reconciliation will pressure you toward Part 6.2's wrong row; one who understands Part 4's distinctions can support the inner work without demanding unsafe relational outcomes.

8.3 FAQ

QuestionAnswer
Can I forgive someone and still testify against them in court or report them to police?Yes. Forgiveness (Part 4.5) releases your personal claim; it does not waive a society's or an institution's legitimate interest in justice and protecting others (Rom 13:1-4 gives civil authority its own, separate role).
Does forgiving mean I have to trust them again?No. Trust is earned behaviorally over time (Part 6.1) and is a completely separate track from forgiveness.
What if they're dead, or I can't reach them?The inner-release half of the process (Part 5.3) is entirely yours to complete regardless; reconciliation simply remains unavailable, which can be grieved (step 6 of Part 5.3) rather than forced.
Is it unforgiving to still feel pain when I remember it?No — Part 2 shows the body's implicit memory updates on its own timeline. Forgiveness is a decision and an ongoing process, not the absence of all future feeling (Part 5.2).
What if I forgave once but the anger came back?Normal and expected (Part 2.4, Part 5.2) — re-choose release again; this is not evidence the first act failed.

8.4 Sources and Limits

Scripture is cited throughout for study. Hebrew and Greek word studies reflect standard lexical sources (e.g., Strong's Concordance, BDB for Hebrew, common New Testament lexicons) and represent well-established, broadly-agreed renderings, though nuance and emphasis vary somewhat between scholars and translations. The neuroscience in Part 2 reflects a genuine and active research area (social pain overlap research associated with Eisenberger and Lieberman; forgiveness-physiology research associated with Worthington, Witvliet, and others) presented at a general, popular level — not a clinical guarantee for any individual, and effect sizes and precise mechanisms remain subjects of ongoing study. The conditional-forgiveness position in Part 7.1 is presented as fairly and fully as possible as a real, sincerely-held Christian position; this document's own resolution (Part 7.3) reflects the relational-gospel framework used throughout this series, offered as one serious reading among others that faithful Christians hold. All named individuals in case studies are composites unless drawn from Scripture, as noted. This is not clinical, legal, or therapeutic advice. If you are in an abusive or dangerous relationship, please involve a trusted professional, counselor, or local protective services before making decisions about reconciliation or contact.
